name: Frailty — exemption evidence engine for Medicaid safety-net providers
one_liner: For the revenue-cycle / patient-access director at a multi-site FQHC, community mental health centre or opioid treatment program, Frailty reads the clinic's own diagnosis, encounter and treatment data against each state's medical-frailty and SUD-treatment exclusion rules, ranks the Medicaid expansion patients most likely to be wrongly disenrolled in the next 60 days, and produces the signed, state-formatted exemption evidence packet for each one.
problem: From 1 January 2027, states must verify that Medicaid expansion adults meet an 80-hours-a-month community-engagement requirement at application and at every six-month renewal (CMS interim final rule, June 2026). Exemptions exist — medically frail, serious/complex conditions, SUD treatment participation, caregivers — but a patient only gets them if the state's data match works or if evidence is produced within a 30-day window. States are building their verification side (Healthy Together CEVS, MedicaidKeeper, Gainwell, Deloitte/Optum systems contracts). Nobody is building the provider side. North Carolina already runs a Tier 1 / Tier 2 code framework where Tier 2 cases require a clinician-signed DSS-8209 medical report routed to the county DSS; Washington's HCA requires a qualifying diagnosis plus an encounter within a 12-month lookback and says it will ask providers for documentation from 2028. MGMA has warned practices to expect medical-frailty documentation requests. Today the clinic's answer is: a front-desk eligibility check discovers the patient has lapsed (Physicians Practice, Oct 2026), a financial counsellor chases paperwork by hand, and the clinician fills a PDF from memory. The clinic eats the visit as uncompensated care. Commonwealth Fund estimates safety-net hospital operating margins fall 1.0-1.1 points (~26-30% of baseline, $4.2-4.7B revenue) under work requirements; NACHC estimates ~$7B of annual community-health revenue reduction from H.R.1 overall.
target_customer: Buyer: VP/Director of Revenue Cycle or Patient Access at a multi-site safety-net provider — 3-20 site FQHC networks, community mental health centres / CCBHCs, and opioid treatment program chains, in the ~44 states (KFF count) that must implement. CFO signs. Champion: the eligibility/outreach-and-enrollment supervisor who owns the navigators. These organisations already pay for Pointcare, Advocatia/Azara, Elevate PFS or Phreesia, so there is a budget line called "eligibility and enrollment".
why_now: The CMS Community Engagement interim final rule (published 3 June 2026) sets a hard 1 January 2027 start, six-month redeterminations and a 30-day cure window — a date-certain deadline, not a trend. Self-attestation is permitted in 2027 in several states but is restricted from 2028, so the documentary burden lands on providers exactly as the 2027 renewal cycles roll. States are publishing frailty code sets now (NC Tier 1/Tier 2; WA HCA diagnosis+utilisation memo based on a Harvard methodology), which makes "clinic data → state rule → evidence packet" a computable problem for the first time. This is the narrow wedge inside YC W27's "AI for City Hall"-adjacent and "Plaid for Government Benefits" signal (Gustaf Alströmer, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#plaid-for-government-benefits) — but sold to the provider that loses money, not to the agency. It also fits a16z's "AI reinforces business models" (David Haber) in that the product is paid for out of revenue it protects.
comparables: Healthy Together CEVS (healthytogether.co/medicaid-cevs) — enrollee hour-logging and document upload, sold as an annual licence to state Medicaid agencies; serves the state, not the clinic. MedicaidKeeper — supplemental enrollee/caseworker portal at ~$1 per enrollee per year, again state-side (CBPP vendor landscape). Gainwell, Deloitte, Accenture, Optum — incumbent state eligibility-system contractors; states are spending ~$20M (Iowa), ~$12M (Illinois) on system changes, all agency-side. Milliman Frailty Framework — claims-based frailty determination sold to states, not a provider workflow. Azara Healthcare + Advocatia (azarahealthcare.com, >1,000 safety-net organisations) — closest provider-side player: registries, redetermination outreach, coverage documentation; no published medical-frailty exemption or state attestation-form generation. Pointcare — coverage monitoring and renewal outreach for CHCs; a company profile mentions a patient app for tracking qualifying hours and uploading documents, so this is the most likely fast-follower. Elevate PFS, Firstsource — outsourced eligibility/enrollment services for hospitals, people-heavy and focused on converting self-pay to coverage rather than keeping existing patients covered. Gap: no product found that takes the clinic's own diagnosis + encounter data, applies a specific state's Tier 1/Tier 2 or diagnosis-plus-utilisation rule, and emits the signed state form. Perplexity explicitly could not verify any such product.
market_note: Estimate, clearly labelled. ~1,400 FQHC organisations plus roughly 2,500-3,500 CMHC/CCBHC and OTP organisations in expansion states; call it ~3,000 realistic targets. If a 10,000-patient organisation pays $25k-$75k/year (my planning estimate — no public price benchmark exists for eligibility-support software; Perplexity could not find published FQHC pricing for Pointcare, Advocatia or Elevate PFS), that is a $75M-$220M addressable software line, before any contingency/per-packet pricing. The willingness-to-pay anchor is not software comparables but avoided loss: Commonwealth Fund puts safety-net hospital revenue loss at $4.2-4.7B/yr; a clinic that saves 200 patients × ~$900 of annual Medicaid revenue per patient covers a $75k contract several times over (estimate). Equifax's social-service verification is priced at $22.95-$59.95 per employer record to the requesting agency, which shows public buyers already pay real per-case money for a single verification artefact.
risks: State-by-state rule divergence means the rules engine is 44 small compliance products, not one — expensive to maintain for a solo evening/weekend builder and a natural fit for an incumbent with a services arm. Azara/Advocatia or Pointcare can add "exemption flags" to an existing contract and foreclose the wedge. Political risk: litigation is live (a June 2026 multi-state complaint against the rule) and a court or a future administration could soften the requirement, collapsing the deadline that makes the product urgent.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That providers, not states, end up carrying the documentation load. Several states allow self-attestation through 2027 and plan automated claims matching; if state data matching works well, the 2027 volume is small and the real market starts in 2028 — a year of runway risk. 2) That a revenue-cycle director will pay software prices for a problem whose cost is diffuse (uncompensated visits spread over months) rather than a visible invoice. 3) That the builder can get repeatable data access: FHIR bulk export and Azara/Relevant feeds vary by EHR, and 42 CFR Part 2 makes SUD-treatment participation data legally awkward to move without patient consent — the OTP wedge may need a consent flow before it ships.
first_customers: The first ten are multi-site safety-net organisations in states that have already published a frailty code framework and provider form — start with North Carolina (DSS-8209, Tier 1/Tier 2 live) and Washington (HCA diagnosis+utilisation memo), then Louisiana, Michigan, Illinois, Arizona. Reach them through state primary care associations (NC Community Health Center Association, Washington Association for Community Health), the NACHC work-requirements working groups, Azara DRVS user community (Azara serves >1,000 safety-net orgs and runs user meetings), and the CCBHC/OTP side via state behavioral health provider associations. Cold-open with the one artefact they do not have: a free "how many of your expansion patients look Tier 1 under your state's list" analysis from a CSV they already export.
validation_test: This week: take North Carolina's published Tier 1/Tier 2 code list and Washington's HCA frailty memo, build a one-page scorer, and ask five revenue-cycle or eligibility directors at NC/WA FQHCs and CMHCs for a de-identified CSV of active Medicaid expansion patients (patient ID, diagnosis codes, last encounter date, next renewal month). Return a ranked at-risk list plus three pre-filled DSS-8209 drafts. Pass = at least 3 of 5 send the file within 10 days, and at least 2 say in writing they would pay for this monthly and name a budget owner. Fail = they say the state will handle it or they cannot get the extract — in which case the state-side or MCO-side buyer is the real one.
build_plan: Stack: TypeScript + a small Node/Next service, Postgres, Claude/GPT for the narrative sections of the form, no EHR integration in v1. Steps: (1) Encode two state rule packs as data — NC Tier 1/Tier 2 code list + DSS-8209 field map, WA diagnosis-plus-12-month-utilisation logic; (2) ingest a CSV extract (patient ID, ICD-10s, encounter dates/types, renewal month, program enrollment flag) — no FHIR, no integrations; (3) score each patient: likely-exempt via data match / needs clinician attestation / no exemption path, ranked by renewal date; (4) generate the state-formatted PDF per patient with diagnosis, supporting encounters and dates pre-filled, leaving only the clinician's functional-impairment sentence and signature; (5) a worklist with status tracking (sent to clinician, signed, submitted to DSS, confirmed) and a weekly "patients whose 30-day cure window opens next week" digest. Cut from v1: any direct state submission, hour-logging for working patients, patient-facing app, HIPAA-grade EHR integrations, every state but two, and anything touching 42 CFR Part 2 SUD records.
reasoning: Tonight's bookmarks are almost entirely AI-developer-tool noise (agentic IDEs, agentic TPMs, font generation, Grok shopping), and the two with real substance — Basecamp's Claude connector and the Claude Code review article — point straight at territory the library already covers (Ledger, Doublecheck, SkillProof, Driftwatch). So the winner came from pairing an investor signal with a buyer outside software. YC's "Plaid for Government Benefits" and "AI for City Hall" both describe the same underlying failure: proof-of-eligibility paperwork that agencies cannot automate and people cannot produce. The non-obvious move is to sell not to the agency (slow procurement, incumbents hold the systems contracts) and not to the enrollee (no money), but to the safety-net provider who loses revenue when the patient is disenrolled — and whose own EHR already holds the evidence that would have granted the exemption. That is a buyer with an existing "eligibility and enrollment" budget line, a hard deadline of 1 January 2027, and no product serving the specific workflow: every vendor I could verify is either state-side (Healthy Together CEVS, MedicaidKeeper, Milliman, Gainwell) or provider-side but focused on renewals and self-pay conversion (Pointcare, Advocatia/Azara, Elevate PFS). Perplexity explicitly could not find a product that applies a state's frailty code framework to a clinic's own data and emits the signed state form. It does not reach 8 and I will not pretend it does: market_pull is capped at 7 because I found no published price any provider pays for this specific capability and no job post or RFP for it, and wedge is 7 because the first version depends on getting clinical data extracts out of clinics, which is slower than a self-serve signup and sits at the edge of this builder's UiPath/TypeScript comfort zone. This is not a repeat of Backcheck (city plan-check resubmittals for architects) — different buyer, different regulator, different artefact.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1) Frailty — exemption evidence engine for safety-net providers (PICK): named buyer with an existing eligibility budget line, a date-certain federal deadline, and a confirmed hole between state-side vendors and provider-side outreach tools. 2) Agent write-audit for SMB SaaS connectors (from the Basecamp-for-Claude bookmark): dropped at screen — too close to past ideas Ledger/Doublecheck/SkillProof, same buyer and workflow. 3) Serro-adjacent "spec drift" detector for coding agents: dropped at screen — crowded (Serro itself just launched), developer-tools buyer, and overlaps Driftwatch. 4) Creator-discovery/licensing ops from the typesafeai bookmark: dropped at screen — repeat of Rightsline in buyer and workflow. 5) Font/brand-asset generation as a service (nutlope bookmark): dropped at generate — a weekend build, not a venture, and no B2B buyer with a budget. 6) Employer-side "hours verification letter" desk for hourly employers (staffing, home care, restaurants) under Medicaid work rules: finalist — researched; killed because CMS places verification duty on states and employees, Equifax already covers large employers free, and I found no evidence of an employer-side surge. 7) MCO/health-plan member-retention analytics for work requirements: finalist — researched; competitors already moving (Command Direct + GoMo Health partnership targets exactly this, plus Advocatia's health-plan line), long enterprise sales cycle, poor fit for a solo evening/weekend builder's first sale. 8) County DSS caseworker triage tool for work-requirement documents: dropped at screen — government procurement, 12-18 month sales cycle, incumbents (Deloitte, Gainwell, Optum) hold the systems contracts. 9) "Plaid for benefits" consent-based income verification: dropped at screen — Truv, SteadyIQ, Equifax Complete Income already sell precisely this. 10) AI permit-correction packager for small contractors (from the AI-for-City-Hall signal): dropped at screen — PermitFlow and Pulley are well funded and selling the same workflow, and it is close to the library's Backcheck.

PROJECT
1. Fontsmith — prompt → a real downloadable TTF, riding @nutlope's $0.02 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash fonts. Dropped at screen: YoFont, Mixfont, Lipi.ai and FontDance already do prompt-to-TTF with free tiers, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash is text-out only so the hard part (actual glyph outlines) isn't solved by the new model. Also it is nutlope's own launch — cloning it is out.
2. Voicecheck / one-sentence compass — Caro's "get the book down to one sentence", applied to a README or blog post: infer the thesis, score each section's drift. Finalist. Lost: too close in spirit and audience to Voiceprint (filed yesterday, writing-quality scoring on your own text), and the output is a critique, which is not postable.
3. Creatorscope — paste a niche, get small creators with outsized engagement, from the $0.002/creator UGC discovery post. Dropped at screen: Social Champ's free engagement calculator, Kolsquare's free extension, Heepsy and Tokfluence already cover this, and the underlying creator data isn't free or static-page friendly.
4. Jevmeter — score every function in your repo with a yes/no question. Dropped at screen: "every" already exists in the Jev ecosystem doing exactly this, and it is a repeat of the Skillscale/SkillPeek developer-repo-analysis lane.
5. HN Wrapped-style profile card from a username. Dropped at screen: HN Wrapped 2025 already did it (313 points on Show HN) and Simon Willison published the comment-fetching tool; straight repeat.
6. Threadsort — rank every comment in an HN thread by signal using Jev. Dropped at screen: "HN Jev Sorter" already classifies HN comments in real time.
7. Mentionscope — find every HN/Reddit mention of your product with sentiment. Dropped at screen: F5Bot is free forever for alerts, ShovelScout does the "someone is asking for this" angle free up to 10/day, KWatch has a free tier. Crowded.
8. Ghostread — decode an HN job post's red flags. Dropped at screen: JDDecoder does buzzword/toxicity/ghost-risk free 3/day, MintCareer does ghost-risk free.
9. Agentjobs — a monthly index of who is hiring for agent engineering. Dropped at screen: the Agentic AI Jobs Index (getreadyforagents.com/jobs) already does exactly this, weekly, with downloadable CSV.
10. Hiringscope — paste three lines about yourself, score all ~400 posts in this month's HN hiring thread, ranked with reasons, plus a shareable market-read card. PICK.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Addy Osmani X article (turned out to be Claude Code's code-review process — interesting but squarely in the library's existing agent-reliability territory, so it generated no new candidate), the Basecamp-for-Claude connector (confirmed read/write MCP access as the signed-in user — inspired candidate 2, which I then dropped as a repeat of Ledger/Doublecheck), and Serro (confirmed it already occupies the agentic-TPM slot, killing candidate 3). Screening pot (6/6): checked permit software (PermitFlow, Pulley — killed candidate 10), UGC/creator licensing (killed candidate 4 as a Rightsline repeat), MCP agent audit (killed candidate 2), the Plaid-for-benefits space (found SteadyIQ, Truv — killed candidate 9 and surfaced the Medicaid thread), Medicaid work-requirement vendor landscape, and hospital/FQHC financial exposure. Deep pot (12/12): CBPP's February 2026 vendor landscape (Healthy Together ~$1/enrollee/yr, MedicaidKeeper, Equifax at up to ~$15/income report); Commonwealth Fund safety-net hospital margin estimates; the employer-side hypothesis (candidate 6 — killed: CMS puts the duty on states and enrollees, Equifax is free to employers); provider-attestation mechanics in NC and WA; FQHC vendor landscape and pricing (no public benchmarks — this is why market_pull is capped at 7); NC Health News on county DSS vacancies and 732,000 affected North Carolinians; Physicians Practice on front-desk lapses; the MCO/health-plan angle (candidate 7 — killed: Command Direct/GoMo Health already there); OTP and 42 CFR Part 2 constraints; EHR integration feasibility. Sharpening pot (5/5, folded into the deep calls above on competitor absence, state rule publication, MGMA/NACHC provider warnings, FQHC contract sizing and behavioral-health buyer identification). Investor signals weighed: "Plaid for Government Benefits" (chosen, but inverted to the provider buyer rather than the agency), "AI for City Hall" (used only to kill candidate 10 after finding PermitFlow/Pulley), "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (considered as a framing for navigator tooling, no distinct buyer found), a16z "AI reinforces business models" (supports the pay-from-protected-revenue pricing) and "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" (matches the CSV-pilot go-to-market). No image was interpreted; all bookmark media was video thumbnails with empty alt text.
Sharpening (7 to 7.6): Round 1 — weakest criteria at first scoring: gap 7, market_pull 6 (average 7.0). The original candidate was a general "help Medicaid enrollees prove compliance" tool, which runs straight into Healthy Together CEVS, MedicaidKeeper and Gainwell, all selling to states. Change to the idea: move the buyer from the state/enrollee to the provider that loses revenue, and narrow the workflow from "all compliance" to the single step with the most pain and the least coverage — the medically-frail / SUD exemption evidence packet. Research (CBPP vendor landscape; Azara/Advocatia, Pointcare, Elevate PFS positioning; a targeted search for any EHR-to-attestation product) found every verified competitor is either state-side or provider-side-but-renewal-focused, and found no product generating state attestation forms from clinic data. Gap 7 → 8, market_pull 6 → 7 (lifted only to 7, not higher, because I could not find a published price or a job posting for this exact capability). Round 2 — weakest remaining: wedge 6. Change: anchor v1 on two states that have already published machine-readable rules (NC Tier 1/Tier 2 + DSS-8209; WA HCA diagnosis-plus-utilisation memo) and on a CSV extract instead of EHR integration, so a first paid pilot is weeks not quarters. Research confirmed NC's published tiered code list and provider report routed to county DSS, and WA's published memo and 12-month lookback, plus that FHIR bulk export is uneven across safety-net EHRs so CSV really is the pragmatic path. Wedge 6 → 7; held below 8 because the first sale still requires a data-sharing conversation with a healthcare organisation, not a credit card. Also confirmed in round 2 that MGMA warned practices to expect frailty documentation requests and Physicians Practice described lapses surfacing at the front desk — that evidence lifted pain 7 → 8. Timing scored 10 on the confirmed statutory date (1 Jan 2027) in the CMS interim final rule. Average after sharpening 7.6.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the nutlope DeepSeek V4.1 Flash font post (confirmed the model is text-out, $0.30/$1.20 per M, fonts not yet released — killed candidate 1), the TypeSafe Jev model behind the Typesafe UGC post (confirmed typed decisions, $0.042/M input, output free, OpenRouter availability — this became the engine for the pick), and the Addy Osmani article (subagents vs single agent; produced no candidate).
Screening pot (5/5): one check each on AI font generators (YoFont/Mixfont/Lipi/FontDance — dead), free creator engagement tools (Social Champ, Kolsquare — dead), free thesis/one-sentence writing tools (gap exists but output isn't postable), Jev's browser/CORS and key-exposure story (needs a tiny proxy or BYO key — fed straight into the build plan), and the Jev consumer-app landscape (X Scanner, commit-miner, "every" — killed the repo-scoring candidate).
Deep research pot (8/8): confirmed Jev supports a typed score question with a probability distribution, ~0.10s latency, 262k context, and a warning that text over ~32kB drops into a slower long-context mode (so per-job requests, not one giant request); confirmed HN Algolia is free, keyless, CORS-friendly, 10k req/hr, and supports pulling a whole thread by story id; mapped prior art for HN hiring tools (hnhiring.com, hackernewstrends.com, hntrends.com, MaxwellVolz/hn_whos_hiring, wantstobehired.com, HN Match), for mention-tracking (F5Bot, ShovelScout, KWatch, Syften — killed candidate 7), for JD red-flag decoding (JDDecoder, MintCareer — killed candidate 8), and for agent-job indexes (Agentic AI Jobs Index — killed candidate 9). The decisive finding: the only resume×whole-thread scorer is local-only and subscription-bound, leaving the hosted version open.
Sharpening pot (2/4): checked whether HN hiring trend dashboards already exist (they do — so the trend line is a supporting detail, not the hook) and whether personal-stat cards built from HN data spread (HN Wrapped 2025, 313 points on Show HN — yes, on HN at least). Both findings changed the idea: trends demoted to one line on the card, the card promoted to the shareable artefact. Two sharpening calls unused because the second round's evidence was already conclusive.
Sharpening (7.8 to 8.4): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (7). The v1 was "rank this month's thread for me", which is a once-a-month single-use ranking and arguably a one-time toy if you're not job hunting. Change to the idea: added the "market read" card — a score distribution for the whole thread against you, the one skill most present in jobs that scored you LOW, and a month-over-month delta. This turns it from a job search tool into a "how does the market see me this month" check that employed people also open. Research (Web Summary on HN hiring trend dashboards) found hackernewstrends.com and hntrends.com already chart technology mentions across threads back to 2011 — so trend data is not novel by itself, but neither site ties it to an individual, and the "skill you lack that's blocking your low scorers" view is not present in either. Usefulness 7 → 8.
Round 2 — weak criterion: shareability (7). A ranked job list is private and slightly embarrassing to post. Change: made the market card the shareable artefact, not the list — a screenshot-shaped card with your score vs the whole thread and the delta line, deliberately resembling a stat card rather than a job search. Research (Web Summary on HN Wrapped / Simon Willison profiling HN users) confirmed personal-stat-from-HN-data artefacts spread on HN: HN Wrapped 2025 hit 313 points on Show HN and people shared generated profiles. That's evidence the format spreads, though HN-specific and not proof of broad virality — so shareability 7 → 8, not 9.
Wow held at 8 rather than 9: the output is a ranked list plus a stat card, impressive but not screen-record material; the live cost counter ticking to half a cent while 412 jobs are scored is the closest thing to a 9 moment and is specced in.
prototype_summary: A clickable Frailty prototype showing a ranked Medicaid exemption worklist for a 4-site NC FQHC, where clicking an amber patient turns raw EHR rows into a pre-filled, citable DSS-8209-style medical frailty report ready for clinician signature.
